the-single-core-bottleneck.core: By default a NIC might deliver all packets through one queue, one interrupt and one CPU core. That core does interrupt handling, softirq protocol processing (IP, TCP) and possibly the application, so throughput caps at what one core can handle (often a few Gbps or around 1 Mpps) while other cores idle. Network scaling techniques spread receive and transmit work across cores while keeping each flow's packets in order on one core.

first_principles.problem: A 25 Gbps server tops out at 6 Gbps with CPU 0 at 100% softirq.

analogy.title: One toll booth on a motorway
analogy.story: However wide the road, one booth limits traffic; open more booths and assign each car a lane by plate number.
analogy.breaks: Booths are physical; queue counts are configurable.

code.text:
mpstat -P ALL 1 1 | sort -k8 -n | tail -3    # %soft per CPU
ethtool -l eth0          # Combined: 1 (max 16)
grep eth0 /proc/interrupts | wc -l

check.q: Why can't packets simply be sprayed randomly across all cores?
check.a: Packets of the same flow must be processed in order; random distribution would cause reordering, hurting TCP performance.

hardware-scaling-rss-receive-side-scalin.core: RSS is a NIC feature. Multiple receive queues, each with its own interrupt, and a hash (usually Toeplitz over source and destination IP and ports) choose the queue per packet via an indirection table. Bind each queue's IRQ to a different core and packet processing spreads across them while flows stay on one core. Configure the queue count (ethtool -L), hash fields (ethtool -N rx-flow-hash) and indirection weights (ethtool -X).

first_principles.problem: A NIC supports 16 queues but the driver defaulted to 4, limiting throughput.

analogy.title: A sorting machine at the post office entrance
analogy.story: It reads postcodes and sends letters to different sorting desks, always the same desk for the same postcode.
analogy.breaks: Sorting machines are fixed; RSS hash keys and tables are tunable.

code.text:
ethtool -L eth0 combined 16
ethtool -N eth0 rx-flow-hash udp4 sdfn     # hash UDP on IPs + ports
ethtool -x eth0 | head
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E 'rx_queue_[0-9]+_packets' | head

check.q: Why include UDP ports in the RSS hash?
check.a: Without ports, all traffic between the same two IPs lands on one queue, so ports add spread for many UDP flows.

software-scaling-rps-receive-packet-stee.core: RPS is RSS in software. After the driver receives a packet on one CPU, the kernel computes a flow hash and enqueues the packet to another CPU's backlog (per /sys/class/net/<dev>/queues/rx-N/rps_cpus), where the protocol processing runs. It's useful for NICs with few or no hardware queues, virtual NICs, or to spread processing beyond the queue count, at the cost of an inter-processor interrupt and some cache movement.

first_principles.problem: A VM's virtio NIC has a single queue, so all network processing lands on one vCPU.
truths: The kernel can hash and redistribute.

analogy.title: A receptionist redistributing letters
analogy.story: One person receives all mail at the door, then hands each batch to a different desk by postcode.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists don't interrupt colleagues; RPS sends IPIs.

code.text:
echo ff > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus      # CPUs 0-7
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus
mpstat -P ALL 1 1 | awk '{print $3, $8}' | head   # %soft spreads

check.a: When the NIC has fewer hardware queues than cores (or only one, like many virtual NICs), so the kernel spreads processing in software.

locality-scaling-rfs-receive-flow-steeri.core: RSS and RPS spread flows across CPUs by hash, but the application thread consuming a flow may run on a different CPU, so packet data must move across caches. RFS records which CPU last called recv() for each flow (in a global flow table sized by rps_sock_flow_entries) and steers that flow's packets to that CPU. Accelerated RFS (aRFS) programs the NIC to do it in hardware. Better cache locality lowers latency.

first_principles.problem: Network latency is higher than expected because packets are processed on one core and consumed by a thread on another.
truths: Data processed far from its consumer causes cache misses.
The kernel can learn where consumers run.

analogy.title: Delivering parcels to the desk where the recipient actually sits
analogy.story: Instead of a fixed mailbox by surname, the post finds where the person is working today.
analogy.breaks: People move between desks; threads that migrate a lot reduce RFS benefit.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Packets processed where the app consumes them.

code.text:
sysctl -w net.core.rps_sock_flow_entries=32768
for q in /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-*; do echo 2048 > $q/rps_flow_cnt; done
ethtool -K eth0 ntuple on      # aRFS if supported

check.q: What problem does RFS solve that RSS doesn't?
check.a: RSS picks a CPU by hash; RFS steers packets to the CPU where the consuming application thread runs, improving cache locality.

transmit-side-scaling-xps-transmit-packe.core: On transmit, multi-queue NICs have several TX queues. XPS maps CPUs (or RX queues) to TX queues so each CPU transmits on its own queue, avoiding lock contention on a shared queue and keeping completion processing local. Configure it via /sys/class/net/<dev>/queues/tx-N/xps_cpus (or xps_rxqs). Without it, many cores contend on the same TX queue lock, limiting throughput.

first_principles.problem: A multi-core sender shows high spinlock contention in the network transmit path.

analogy.title: Separate checkout lanes per cashier for departures
analogy.story: Instead of every departing shopper squeezing through one exit gate, each cashier has their own.
analogy.breaks: Exits are physical; XPS mappings are bitmasks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each CPU transmits on its own queue.

code.text:
n=$(ls -d /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/tx-* | wc -l)
for i in $(seq 0 $((n-1))); do
  printf '%x' $((1 << i)) > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/tx-$i/xps_cpus
done
tc qdisc show dev eth0 | head -3     # mq root with per-queue children

check.a: Which CPUs (or RX queues) use which transmit queues, so each CPU sends on its own TX queue without contention.
